questions.q: Kevin's team will build a school management app: students, classes, fees and results. It is not yet clear which questions will come later. Which database should they start with?
questions.hint: Are students, classes and fees separate, or linked to one another?

options.text: A document database, because the schema will keep changing and fixed tables are a hassle
options.why: Changing a schema is easy in relational with migrations. But the joins across linked data and the fee transactions would have to be hand-built in a document database.

options.text: A relational database, because the data is linked and the questions are not known in advance
options.why: Linked data, money and unknown future questions: all three are relational strengths.

options.text: A wide-column database, because it will be easy to scale when users grow
options.why: One school's data will fit on one server for many years. Giving up joins and ad-hoc queries for a problem that may never arrive is a bad trade.

options.text: A graph database, because students and classes have relationships
options.why: One or two steps of relationship are handled by relational foreign keys. A graph is for questions that go many steps deep.

questions.q: Which of these jobs suit a key-value store such as Redis?
questions.hint: Which jobs have a key known in advance and can be rebuilt if the data is lost?

options.text: The session of a logged-in user
options.why: The session ID is the key, reads and writes are very frequent, and you need a TTL. This is the ideal key-value job.

options.text: A per-minute counter of how many requests each client made
options.why: Fast increments by key and automatic expiry are exactly what a rate-limit counter needs.

options.text: A monthly sales report by state
options.why: It needs to scan many rows with joins and GROUP BY. A key-value store cannot search inside its values at all.

options.text: A cache of a computed product page
options.why: It is read by product ID, and if lost it can be rebuilt from the main database.

options.text: The primary records of orders and payments
options.why: These are the source of truth. They need transactions, constraints and many kinds of queries, which a key-value store does not offer.

questions.q: In a factory, 5 thousand sensors send a temperature every 10 seconds. The dashboard must show "the hourly average for the last 24 hours". Which family fits this data best?
questions.hint: Does the data change, or is it only appended? And what is the query about?

options.text: A graph database
options.why: There are no relationships to walk here, just measurements arriving over time.

options.text: A key-value store
options.why: It reads only by key. A time-window calculation like an hourly average over 24 hours is not its job.

options.text: A time-series database
options.why: A timestamp and a measurement, append-only, queried by time window: that is the very definition of time-series. With TimescaleDB you can start inside PostgreSQL.

options.text: A document database
options.why: You could store it there, but you would have to build time partitioning, compression and old-data deletion yourself.

questions.q: A team keeps the "main" copy of each order in two databases. What is the biggest problem with this code?
questions.hint: What if the server dies after the first write succeeds but before the second?

options.text: flush() is slow, so it should write to MongoDB first
options.why: Reversing the order has the same danger: one can succeed and the other fail. The problem is not the order but writing separately to two places.

options.text: If the second write fails, the two databases hold different truths, and there is no way to tell which is right
options.why: This is a dual write. The two writes cannot be bound into one transaction, and since no source of truth is defined, a mismatch cannot be settled either.

options.text: There is no problem: data in two places is safer
options.why: Safety comes from backups and replication. Two "main" copies create the risk of disagreement instead.

options.text: It should use the Serializer instead of toArray()
options.why: That is a matter of code taste; it does not change the core risk of the data drifting apart in the slightest.

questions.q: In which situations is adding a second database a reasonable decision?
questions.hint: Which reasons can be measured, and which are only wishes?

options.text: One specific query was measured as slow, and indexes and caching did not fix it
options.why: There is a measured pain and the easy options are used up: this is the right moment for a new database.

options.text: Big companies use that database
options.why: Their load is not your load. Their solution may just be extra running cost for you.

options.text: If the new database loses its data, it can be rebuilt from the main database
options.why: Then it is derived data and there is still only one source of truth, so the risk stays under control.

options.text: One person on the team wants to learn the new technology
options.why: The place for learning is a side project. In production the whole team carries its backups, monitoring and night-time incidents.

questions.q: A shop has attributes that differ by product type (phone RAM, shirt size). All its other data (orders, customers, payments) is interlinked. Which design is best?
questions.hint: Does a small part of the app justify replacing the whole database?

options.text: Move the entire app to a document database
options.why: Losing order and payment transactions and joins to gain the convenience of one column is a bad trade.

options.text: Create a separate nullable column for every possible attribute
options.why: You would get hundreds of mostly empty columns, and every new kind of product would need a migration.

options.text: Keep a JSON column on the product table in the relational database
options.why: Fixed facts go in strict columns, the varying attributes go in JSON: both benefits in one database, with indexing.

options.text: Put the attributes in a separate document database and the rest in PostgreSQL
options.why: Splitting one product's data across two databases brings syncing, backup and mismatch trouble, when a JSON column does the job.

questions.q: A chat app writes 200 thousand messages per second. It is read in only one way: "the last 50 messages of this conversation". A single-server relational database cannot keep up with the writes. Which family fits best?
questions.hint: The write load is huge, but there is just one query and it is known in advance.

options.text: A wide-column database, with the conversation ID as the partition key
options.why: Huge write volume spreads across many servers, and the only query goes by the partition key. This is exactly what wide-column is built for.

options.text: A graph database, because people are talking to each other
options.why: The question is not about walking relationships; it is about reading one conversation's messages in order.

options.text: A key-value store, with the conversation ID as the key and the whole chat as one value
options.why: Every new message would rewrite the whole value, and the value would keep growing without bound.

options.text: Buy a bigger relational server
options.why: It will last a while, but one server has a write ceiling. With one known query, paying the price of a distributed database is worth it here.

questions.q: Nicole's team stores each order as one JSON document. Finance now asks: "total sales per state, with each product's current price". What is hard here?
questions.hint: Which part of the data lives in a different document?

options.text: Reading one whole order, because the JSON is too big
options.why: Reading one whole order is exactly what a document is best at: one read returns everything.

options.text: Combining orders with the current product prices, because joins across documents are not built in
options.why: The price lives in the product documents. The team has to fetch and match them in code, which a relational join does in one statement.

options.text: Saving a new order, because documents cannot be added
options.why: Adding a document is trivial and fast; writes are not the weakness here.

questions.q: A table has customer_address copied into every order row. The customer changes their address. What problem arises?
questions.hint: Where else is the address written?

options.text: Old orders keep the old address and new ones get the new one; it is hard to tell which is the real address
options.why: When the same fact lives in many places, one change leaves the rest stale. This is the update anomaly.

options.text: Nothing, because the database updates every row by itself
options.why: The database does not know which columns are copies of the same fact. It treats separate columns as separate facts.

options.text: Only the database size grows a little, with no other problem
options.why: The storage cost is not the real problem; the real problem is the data disagreeing with itself.

options.text: The table can no longer be written to
options.why: Writes keep working, but with wrong or stale facts. The problem grows silently.

questions.q: Which of these are traits of a normalized design?
questions.hint: How many homes should each fact have?

options.text: The order holds customer_id, and the name and phone live in the customer table
options.why: The fact lives once in its owner's table, and the order holds only the ID.

options.text: One column holds several phone numbers separated by commas
options.why: It breaks the rule of one value per cell; you would need a separate phone table.

options.text: Changing a name means changing only one row
options.why: Because the fact exists once, one change shows the new value everywhere.

options.text: Every order has customer_name copied in so that no join is needed
options.why: That is a copying (denormalized) design, and its biggest risk is disagreement.

questions.q: Two users sign up with the same email at the very same moment. What can happen with the code below?
questions.hint: What if both requests get past the "look first" step?

options.text: Both pass and two accounts get created, if the database has no UNIQUE constraint
options.why: Both requests see "not found" at the same time, then both write. A UNIQUE constraint would have blocked the second write.

options.text: Nothing, because findOneBy() takes a lock in the database
options.why: A plain findOneBy() takes no lock; it only reads.

options.text: flush() will catch the duplicate by itself
options.why: flush() just sends SQL. Catching duplicates takes a UNIQUE index in the database.

options.text: A problem occurs only if the emails differ in upper and lower case
options.why: It is not about spelling; the real risk is two requests arriving together.

questions.q: The product_id foreign key on order_item has onDelete: RESTRICT. What happens when you try to delete a product that is in an order?
questions.hint: Think about what the word RESTRICT means.

options.text: The order_item rows for that product are deleted too
options.why: That is CASCADE behavior. RESTRICT is the exact opposite.

options.text: The product_id on the order_item becomes NULL by itself
options.why: That is SET NULL behavior, and it would not even work on a NOT NULL column.

options.text: The database blocks the delete and raises an error
options.why: RESTRICT means that as long as another row refers to it, it cannot be deleted. History never ends up orphaned.

options.text: The delete goes through and the order_item is left holding an orphan ID
options.why: An FK exists precisely to prevent orphan rows like this.

questions.q: In which cases is copying data (denormalizing) reasonable?
questions.hint: Which value should stay fixed in old records even after it changes?

options.text: The price of each product on an invoice, as of the moment of the order
options.why: History has to stay fixed. Joining the current price would change the totals of old invoices.

options.text: The customer's current name on every order, so no join is needed
options.why: It is meant to always show the current name; the copy will go stale and cause disagreement.

options.text: The delivery address as it was when the order was placed
options.why: Even if the address changes later, where the old parcel went is part of history.

options.text: Any column at all, because joins are always slow
options.why: A join is usually fast when indexed. Copying without measuring only adds risk.

questions.q: Steven's phone is copied into every order row. A developer runs the UPDATE below. What goes wrong?
questions.code:
UPDATE customer_order SET customer_phone = '555-0102'
WHERE customer_name = 'Steven Miller';
questions.hint: Look at how the name was typed in the other rows.

options.text: Rows where the name was typed differently ("Stephen Miller") are missed and keep the old number
options.why: With copies, you find them by matching text, and any variant slips through. One person ends up with two numbers.

options.text: Nothing, the UPDATE fixes every row of that customer
options.why: It fixes only rows whose text matches exactly.

options.text: The database refuses because the column is duplicated
options.why: The database has no idea the columns are copies of one fact; it just runs the UPDATE.

options.text: It is slow, but the result is correct
options.why: Speed is not the issue; the missed rows are.

questions.q: Ryan's query is WHERE customer_id = 42 AND status = 'paid' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. Which composite index is best?
questions.hint: Equality columns first, the sorting column last.

options.text: (created_at, customer_id, status)
options.why: With the sorting column first, you cannot jump straight to customer_id. Every row has to be examined.

options.text: (status, created_at)
options.why: customer_id is missing. status has only a few distinct values, so it cuts out almost nothing.

options.text: (customer_id, status, created_at)
options.why: The two equality columns come first and the sorting column last. customer_id and status narrow it down, and then 20 rows are taken straight from created_at's sorted order.

options.text: Three separate indexes, one per column
options.why: The database usually picks just one, and the others cannot supply the sort order. Writes cost three times as much.

questions.q: You have an index on (customer_id, created_at). Which of these queries will it help?
questions.hint: Check whether the first column is in the condition.

options.text: WHERE customer_id = 7
options.why: It starts from the leftmost column, so the index helps directly.

options.text: WHERE created_at > '2026-01-01'
options.why: Without the first column there is no way into the index. It breaks the leftmost prefix rule.

options.text: WHERE customer_id = 7 AND created_at > '2026-01-01'
options.why: Equality, then a range. Both columns follow the index order.

options.text: WHERE customer_id = 7 ORDER BY created_at DESC
options.why: Within each customer_id, created_at is sorted, so the result comes back without a separate sort.

questions.q: Looking at this EXPLAIN output, what should you do?
questions.code:
Seq Scan on customer_order
  (actual time=0.02..408.9 rows=20 loops=1)
  Filter: (customer_id = 42)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 1999980
Execution Time: 412.7 ms
questions.hint: How many rows were touched to get 20?

options.text: Create an index on customer_id, then run EXPLAIN again to confirm
options.why: 2 million rows were read for 20. With an index the plan should become an Index Scan, and you verify that in EXPLAIN.

options.text: Add more RAM to the database server
options.why: More RAM would read all the rows faster, but it would still read 2 million of them. The problem is the amount of work.

options.text: Lower the LIMIT to 10
options.why: The problem is in the filter. Reducing the LIMIT leaves the amount of reading almost the same.

options.text: Nothing, 412ms is always fine
options.why: 412ms is a lot for 20 rows, and it will keep growing as rows are added.

questions.q: A log table takes thousands of INSERTs per second and has 8 indexes. What problem will it have?
questions.hint: How many places does each INSERT write to?

options.text: SELECTs will be slow, because more indexes make lookups slower
options.why: More indexes do not usually slow lookups down; they slow writes.

options.text: Every INSERT updates 8 indexes, so writes are slow and more disk is used
options.why: A new entry must be placed in the right spot in every index. On a table written to this often, that is a heavy load.

options.text: Nothing, because indexes live in a separate file
options.why: Even in a separate file, they must be updated on every write.

options.text: The database will drop the extra indexes by itself
options.why: A database never drops your indexes on its own.

questions.q: A company gets 50 million orders a year, mostly "delivered". Queries run frequently, and only on "pending" orders. Which index fits best?
questions.hint: Why keep rows the query never visits in the index?

options.text: A plain index on the status column
options.why: The tens of millions of delivered rows would go into the index too. It gets bigger and slower, though the query never wants them.

options.text: A partial index only for rows where status = 'pending'
options.why: The index stays small, and most writes (orders becoming delivered) barely touch it.

options.text: A separate index on every column
options.why: Write cost multiplies, and none of them is specially small for pending rows.

options.text: No index, just a bigger server
options.why: The root cause is reading the wrong amount of data. A bigger server only hides it.

questions.q: An IoT company's 500 thousand sensors each send a reading every 10 seconds. Reads are rare, and only by time window. Which engine family fits best?
questions.hint: The write load is huge and the data is only appended.

options.text: LSM-based, because writes are collected and appended at the end
options.why: Sequential writes are cheap, and the read pattern is known in advance. This is where an LSM is strong.

options.text: B-tree-based, because a B-tree is always fast
options.why: Under a huge write load, changing scattered pages becomes a burden. There is no such thing as "always fast".

options.text: No engine will work
options.why: LSM-based and time-series databases were built for exactly this kind of job.

options.text: The engine makes no difference, the SQL is the same
options.why: Even if the SQL is the same, the cost of reads and writes depends on the engine.

questions.q: An LSM-based database's writes sometimes suddenly slow down even though traffic is the same. What is the most likely cause?
questions.hint: Which background job eats disk and CPU?

options.text: The WAL was deleted
options.why: If the WAL were deleted you would lose data in a crash; writes would not slow down.

options.text: Compaction is running and taking a big share of the disk
options.why: Merging many files takes disk and CPU, so under extreme load write speed can drop suddenly.

options.text: B-tree pages are splitting
options.why: Page splits belong to B-trees, not to LSM.

options.text: The memtable never goes to disk
options.why: When the memtable fills up, it does go to disk.

questions.q: What is the problem in the code below?
questions.hint: What if the server stops right after you tell the user the payment succeeded?

options.text: No problem, the files don't get corrupted anyway
options.why: Even if the files stay intact, the payment record can be lost after you have told the user "success".

options.text: It is dangerous for money data like payments: the last commit can be lost
options.why: With synchronous_commit off, the WAL can reach the disk a little after the commit. That is not acceptable for money data.

options.text: SET LOCAL is wrong, it should be SET
options.why: SET LOCAL applies to just one transaction, which is the better choice. The problem is elsewhere.

options.text: insert() is slow, executeStatement() should be used
options.why: This is not about slow versus fast; it is about the risk of losing data.

questions.q: A queue consumer inserts 20,000 audit rows, one commit each. At 5 ms per flush it takes 100 seconds. What should Nicole try first?
questions.hint: Which fix makes it faster without risking any data?

options.text: Set fsync = off in postgresql.conf
options.why: It is fast, but a power cut can corrupt the whole database. Far too high a price for an insert loop.

options.text: Insert the rows in chunks of about 1,000, one transaction per chunk
options.why: 20,000 flushes become 20, so about 0.1 s of waiting instead of 100 s, and every committed row is still safely on disk.

options.text: Set synchronous_commit = off for the whole server
options.why: It helps, but every payment on that server could now lose its last commit. Batching comes first, and the setting belongs in one transaction at most.

options.text: Buy more RAM
options.why: The wait is for the disk flush at each commit, not for memory.

questions.q: Which of these statements about the WAL and engines are true?
questions.hint: What does the WAL write first, and why?

options.text: It is written to the WAL first, then to its real place
options.why: This order is what makes recovery after a crash possible.

options.text: Only LSM databases have a WAL
options.why: PostgreSQL and MySQL use a WAL (or redo log) too.

options.text: PostgreSQL and MySQL InnoDB are B-tree based
options.why: Their data and indexes live in sorted B-tree pages.

options.text: Without compaction, an LSM reads at the same speed
options.why: Without compaction, files pile up and a read has to check many of them.

questions.q: A small e-commerce startup says, "Cassandra is fast at writes, so let's build the order database on it." What do you tell them?
questions.hint: What kinds of queries and transactions do orders need?

options.text: Right, fast writes is all that matters
options.why: Giving up joins, transactions and arbitrary queries for speed is a bad trade.

options.text: Start with PostgreSQL; a small app's write load fits on one server, and a B-tree suits linked data
options.why: Orders need joins and transactions. If a measured problem shows up, you can change then.

options.text: Take MongoDB, because it is more popular
options.why: Popularity is not a yardstick for the decision, and the problem here is linked data.

options.text: Take SQLite, because it is a small app
options.why: SQLite is a single-file database and does not suit being the main database of a web app running on several servers.

questions.q: Ryan's table has 200 million rows with a UUIDv4 primary key, and inserts are getting slow. What is the most likely cause?
questions.hint: Where in the index does each new ID land?

options.text: A UUID is 16 bytes, which is too big, so everything is slow
options.why: It adds a little size, but it is not the main reason for the slowdown. The main reason is the lack of order.

options.text: Random IDs land on any page of the index each time, so pages split and cache misses rise
options.why: The lack of order is the cost. Switch to UUIDv7 and new IDs go to the last page.

options.text: The database does not understand UUIDs and treats them as text
options.why: With a native uuid type the database stores it as binary just fine.

options.text: The Symfony Uid component is slow
options.why: Making an ID takes microseconds. The slowness is in the database index.

questions.q: In which of these cases is a sequence (auto-increment) a good enough choice?
questions.hint: Think about whether the ID is shown outside, and how many databases there are.

options.text: One database, with IDs used only internally and never seen by users
options.why: Then there is no guessing or coordination problem. It is small and fast.

options.text: Three databases in different regions feed data into one table
options.why: If each database makes its own 1, 2, 3, the IDs will collide.

options.text: Public URLs like /orders/ID with no ownership check
options.why: It is easy to guess, so the risk is high; you must add authorization first.

options.text: A mobile app creates IDs offline and sends them to the server later
options.why: Offline, it cannot reach the server's sequence; you need a UUID or ULID.

questions.q: Which of these are properties of UUIDv7?
questions.hint: v7 = time + random.

options.text: It starts with 48 bits of millisecond time
options.why: This time is what makes the ID sort in time order.

options.text: It needs no central coordination to create
options.why: Any server or client can make one itself; a collision is practically impossible.

options.text: It is impossible to estimate how far apart in time two IDs were created
options.why: The opposite: the time is right there in the ID, so it can be read.

options.text: It fits in a bigint, 8 bytes
options.why: A UUID is 16 bytes. The 8 bytes belong to a Snowflake.

questions.q: What is the biggest risk in this code?
questions.hint: The UUID is fine, but who checks who is asking?

options.text: A UUID is too long and will break the URL
options.why: 36 characters fit in a URL without trouble.

options.text: There is no ownership check. Anyone who gets hold of another person's invoice UUID can view it
options.why: A UUID can leak. Every request needs an authorization check with a voter or #[IsGranted].

options.text: Requirement::UUID_V7 is wrong, it should be UUID_V4
options.why: If the ID is v7, v7 is right. That is not the problem.

options.text: An entity cannot be returned with json()
options.why: It can, though a DTO is usually better. But that is not the main risk.

questions.q: You need hundreds of thousands of IDs per second, generated on 12 servers, and they must fit in a bigint. What fits, and what care is needed?
questions.hint: You want both small (8 bytes) and sorted by time.

options.text: UUIDv4, no care needed
options.why: v4 is 16 bytes and does not fit in a bigint; being random, it also scatters the index.

options.text: A Snowflake-style ID; give each server a distinct machine id and watch the clock
options.why: 64 bits of time + machine id + counter. The coordination is in the machine id, and a clock that goes backwards can break IDs.

options.text: Each server runs its own sequence
options.why: All 12 servers would make the same numbers and the IDs would collide.

options.text: All servers write to one central sequence
options.why: With hundreds of thousands of requests, that center becomes the bottleneck, and if it fails everything stops.

questions.q: The code below reads right after a write. With a replica in place, what problem can occur, and when?
questions.hint: Which connection will the second request use?

options.text: GET /comments is a new request, so it may read from a replica; if there is lag, the new comment may not show up
options.why: The switch to the primary lasts only within the same request. The next request goes to a replica again, where there may be lag.

options.text: Nothing, because flush() updates all the replicas
options.why: flush() writes only to the primary. Getting changes to the replicas is the database's own job, and it takes time.

options.text: findBy() writes, so it goes to the primary
options.why: findBy() only reads, so it can go to a replica.

options.text: The problem occurs only with sync replication
options.why: Sync reduces the problem, but this exact setup (async with lag) is the commonly used one.

questions.q: Which of these jobs is safe to do from a follower?
questions.hint: What harm is there if the data is slightly stale?

options.text: Generating the month-end sales report
options.why: Data a few seconds old does not change the meaning of a report, and the heavy query spares the leader.

options.text: Showing the product catalog list
options.why: A catalog a few seconds old does no harm. The heavy read load moves to the followers.

options.text: Reading the stock before confirming an order
options.why: Deciding on stale stock can sell the same item twice; this must be read from the leader.

options.text: Showing, in a form, the address the user has just saved
options.why: Their very latest write may not have reached the follower yet; read-your-own-writes would break.

questions.q: A database uses async replication and the leader suddenly crashes. A manager asks whether any data could be lost.
questions.hint: Did the leader wait for a follower before saying "done"?

options.text: No, replication never loses data
options.why: That is a property of sync. Async gives no such guarantee.

options.text: Yes, commits that had not yet reached a follower may be lost
options.why: With async, the leader commits without the followers' confirmation, so changes still on their way can be lost.

options.text: All the data will be lost
options.why: Only the latest part that did not reach a follower; everything earlier is on the follower.

options.text: Only read data is lost, not writes
options.why: There is no read data to lose. The risk is in the written changes.

questions.q: A money-transfer database must never lose data after saying a commit succeeded, yet writes must not stop if one follower dies. Which setup fits?
questions.hint: You want sync, but not dependent on just one follower.

options.text: Async only, because it is fast
options.why: A crash can lose the last commits.

options.text: Three followers, one designated sync follower, the rest async
options.why: If that single sync follower dies, writes get stuck.

options.text: Several followers with ANY 1 style quorum sync: a commit succeeds when any one confirms
options.why: The data is on at least one follower, and if one dies, writes carry on through another.

options.text: No followers, just a good backup
options.why: A backup takes you back to old data; it does not give instant failover or protect the last commits.

questions.q: Because of a network problem, the app thought the leader had died and promoted a follower. The old leader was actually alive. What will happen, and what should have been done?
questions.hint: What if two leaders both take writes?

options.text: Split brain: both take writes and the data divides in two. The old one should have been fenced before the new leader was promoted
options.why: A failover without stopping the old one lets two leaders take writes at once, and merging two ledgers is hard.

options.text: Nothing, the database will reconcile itself
options.why: An ordinary leader/follower setup cannot merge two leaders' writes by itself.

options.text: The database will shut down automatically
options.why: The old leader does not know it has been replaced; it keeps taking writes.

options.text: Only the followers' reads will be wrong, writes will be fine
options.why: The problem is in the writes: two leaders accept two different sets of changes.

questions.q: After a write, Ryan's redirected page often misses his new comment. Which fix actually removes this on the next request?
questions.hint: Doctrine only sticks to the primary inside the request that wrote.

options.text: Remember the write in the session and read from the primary for a few seconds
options.why: It carries the primary connection into the next request, long enough for the replica to catch up. The price is slightly less read offloading.

options.text: Call flush() a second time before redirecting
options.why: flush() writes to the primary only; it does nothing to speed up the replica.

options.text: Add more replicas
options.why: More followers means more copies lagging; it does not fix reading a copy that is behind.

options.text: Switch the database to sync replication for every table
options.why: It would cut the lag, but it slows every write for a problem you can solve for one user at no such cost.

questions.q: Ryan's database is seeing more reads and more writes. What should he do first?
questions.hint: Which step is cheapest?

options.text: Split the data across 4 shards straight away
options.why: This is the most complex and riskiest step. If simpler fixes work, you never need it.

options.text: Measure slow queries and add indexes, then look at a cache and read replicas
options.why: These are cheap and safe, and most problems end here. Only if they fall short do you move to the next step.

options.text: Move the whole app to a new NoSQL database
options.why: That brings a migration and fresh risks, and the real cause of the problem has not even been measured.

options.text: Do nothing and wait
options.why: The problem won't fix itself. Measure first, then try the simple steps.

questions.q: An app uses shard key = created_at (monthly ranges). What happens?
questions.hint: Which shard does today's write go to?

options.text: Writes spread evenly across all shards
options.why: A new row always has today's date, so every new row goes to the same shard.

options.text: All writes hit the latest shard (a hot shard) while the older ones sit nearly idle
options.why: Over time, writes always land in the newest range. That is the classic trap of using a date as a range key.

options.text: No problem, because range queries are easy
options.why: Range queries are easy, but the write load piling onto one shard is the real problem.

options.text: The database will balance the shards by itself
options.why: The database does not balance load on its own; the kind of key decides that.

questions.q: What is wrong with this code?
questions.hint: When % 4 becomes % 5, which shard does the same customer_id go to?

options.text: When the shard count changes, most customers map to a different shard (4 of every 5 here), so most data has to move
options.why: With a direct % N, changing N changes the calculation itself. With virtual buckets only about a fifth of the data moves.

options.text: getConnection() can't be called like this
options.why: ManagerRegistry::getConnection(name) works fine.

options.text: customerId should be a string, not an int
options.why: The type isn't the problem; the calculation changing during resharding is.

options.text: Nothing is wrong
options.why: There is a problem: changing N moves most of the data.

questions.q: Ryan copies bucket 4's rows to shard_4, then flips the map. Customers kept ordering during the copy, and no dual write was on. What goes wrong?
questions.hint: What happened to the orders placed after the copy started?

options.text: Orders placed during the copy exist only on shard_0, so they vanish for the router after the flip
options.why: The copy is a snapshot. Without dual writes (step 1) and a verify (step 3), everything written meanwhile is missing on the new shard.

options.text: Nothing, because the flip copies the rows by itself
options.why: The flip changes one row in the map. It moves no data at all.

options.text: Buckets can only move all at once, never one by one
options.why: One bucket at a time is exactly the point of the map.

options.text: The hash must be recalculated for every customer
options.why: The hash never changes with buckets. Only the map entry for the bucket does.

questions.q: Which tasks get harder in a sharded app?
questions.hint: Think of tasks that need data from several shards at once.

options.text: Joining rows that live on two different shards
options.why: The database can't join tables on separate servers, so the app has to do it.

options.text: Reading all of one customer's orders (shard key = customer_id)
options.why: These all sit on one shard, so it's easy.

options.text: Changing balances in one transaction across two shards
options.why: An ordinary ACID transaction doesn't span shards; you need a saga or another approach.

options.text: Keeping emails unique across the whole system
options.why: A UNIQUE constraint only works within one shard; across the system you need a separate mechanism.

questions.q: A SaaS app has 10,000 tenants, but one tenant's data equals all the others combined. It is sharded by tenant_id. What is the problem and the fix?
questions.hint: Which shard does one enormous tenant land on?

options.text: No problem, hashing spreads everything evenly
options.why: Hashing spreads tenants evenly, but one tenant's data stays on a single shard, so that shard balloons.

options.text: That tenant's shard will run hot; a lookup table can put the giant tenant on its own dedicated shard
options.why: A lookup (directory) strategy lets you place any tenant on any shard. That is the answer to the celebrity problem.

options.text: Change the key to created_at
options.why: Then all new writes go to one shard, and tenant-based queries have to visit every shard.

options.text: Move all tenants back onto one shard
options.why: That throws away the whole point of sharding.

questions.q: Ryan writes a comment and refreshes the page, but his comment is missing. Which guarantee broke?
questions.hint: The problem is about his own write.

options.text: Read-your-writes
options.why: The user did not see their own write on the next read. That is exactly what this guarantee promises.

options.text: Causal consistency
options.why: This isn't about the order of two dependent events; it is about his own write.

options.text: Monotonic reads
options.why: That breaks when older data returns after newer data. Here the newer data was never seen at all.

options.text: None of them; the data was lost
options.why: The data is there; it just hasn't reached the replica that was read.

questions.q: Which of these features needs strong consistency most?
questions.hint: Where could stale data cause a wrong decision?

options.text: A post's like count
options.why: Showing one or two too many or too few hurts nobody.

options.text: A payment-app balance, like Venmo, checked before a spend
options.why: A stale balance could let someone spend twice, and the money would be wrong.

options.text: A blog's read count
options.why: An approximate number is enough; it needn't be exact.

options.text: A "recently viewed products" list
options.why: A list a few seconds old does no harm.

questions.q: What is the problem in this code, assuming reads go to a replica?
questions.hint: Which connection will the request after the redirect use?

options.text: The user may open their profile and see the old address, so it looks like the save failed
options.why: If the new request hits a replica that is behind, read-your-writes breaks. You need the primary for a while after a write, or an LSN check.

options.text: Nothing, because flush() has finished
options.why: flush() writes only to the primary; the replica gets it later.

options.text: Using a redirect is wrong
options.why: The redirect is fine; the issue is where the next read comes from.

options.text: It should use merge() instead of persist()
options.why: This is not an ORM question; it is about which copy the data is read from.

questions.q: Which guarantee do you get easily by always sending a user to the same replica?
questions.hint: One replica never goes back in time, but you don't know how far ahead it is.

options.text: Monotonic reads
options.why: A single replica only moves forward in time, so you never return to older data.

options.text: Read-your-writes
options.why: That replica may not have heard about your write yet, so you need a separate check or the primary.

options.text: Strong consistency
options.why: Even the same replica can lag behind the leader, so there is no guarantee of the latest value.

options.text: None needed: in eventual consistency, time never goes backwards
options.why: In eventual consistency, time can go backwards; a sticky replica reduces that problem.

questions.q: When is causal ordering most likely to break, and how do you handle it?
questions.hint: Where does related data travel by different paths?

options.text: When the question and the answer live on different shards
options.why: The two shards propagate at different speeds, so the answer can arrive first.

options.text: When you read in order from one replica of a single leader
options.why: A single-leader replica preserves write order, so causal ordering is unlikely to break.

options.text: By storing the cause's log position on the reply and reading the question from the primary until the replica reaches it
options.why: When the link to the cause is in the data, the app can make sure the cause is readable before it shows the effect.

options.text: By keeping every comment in its own small file
options.why: Splitting into files scrambles the order even more; keeping the relationship is the fix.

questions.q: A teammate hides, in the browser, every reply whose parent hasn't arrived. Why is that not causal consistency?
questions.hint: Who else reads the reply besides the browser?

options.text: It hides the symptom in one client; emails, API clients and search indexes still get the answer without its question
options.why: Causal order has to be enforced where the data is read, so every consumer gets cause before effect.

options.text: Hiding replies is slower than reading from the primary
options.why: Speed is not the issue; a filter is cheap. The issue is that it only fixes one consumer.

options.text: The browser cannot know which reply belongs to which question
options.why: With a parent id it can know. But knowing the link is not the same as making the cause readable.

questions.q: A controller loads 100 orders with `findBy()` and passes them to this template. There is no fetch join, and each order has a different customer. What is the maximum number of queries that run?
questions.code: {% for order in orders %} {{ order.id }} {{ order.customer.name }} {{ order.items|length }} {% endfor %}
questions.hint: Count how many separate relations the loop touches.

options.why: That one query only loads the orders. Customers and items are not loaded yet, and touching them in the template runs separate queries.
That counts only the 100 customer queries. `order.items|length` also runs one more query per order.
1 for the orders, 100 for the customers and 100 for the items collections: 201 in all.
Queries add up, they don't multiply: each order costs 1 for the customer and 1 for the items.

questions.q: Rachel tried to fix N+1 by joining customer with `->join()` in the repository. The Profiler still shows 51 queries. What is the most likely reason?
questions.hint: Joining and having the joined entity built are two different things.

options.text: `addSelect()` is missing, so the customer's columns never came back and the customer is still a proxy
options.why: `join()` alone just adds a SQL JOIN. Only with `addSelect()` does Doctrine build the joined entity from the same query.

options.text: She should have written `leftJoin()` instead of `join()`
options.why: Inner versus left changes which rows come back, not whether the customer is hydrated.

options.text: The customers table has no index
options.why: An index would make each query faster, but the number of queries would still be 51.

options.text: The cache wasn't cleared
options.why: This is about the shape of the code's queries, nothing to do with a cache.

questions.q: Which of these are effective ways to catch N+1?
questions.hint: No single N+1 query is slow, so which measurement helps?

options.text: Checking the query count for one page in the Symfony Profiler's Doctrine panel
options.why: On a list page, a query count close to the row count is N+1.

options.text: Asserting on the query count in a functional test
options.why: After you fix it once, if someone brings it back, CI catches it.

options.text: Reading the slow log for queries over 1 second
options.why: Every N+1 query finishes in milliseconds, so not one of them appears in the slow log.

options.text: Checking the log for the same `SELECT … WHERE id = ?` running again and again
options.why: Row after row of the same-looking query, differing only in the id, is the best-known sign of N+1.

questions.q: 50 orders, each with 4 items and 3 payments. If you fetch-join both collections, items and payments, in one query, how many rows does the database return?
questions.hint: When two collections are joined together, do an order's rows add up or multiply?

options.why: Once you join a collection, an order no longer fits in one row.
That is 50 × (4 + 3). But the rows of two collections don't add: every item pairs with every payment.
50 × 4 × 3 = 600. That is the cartesian product, and the reason to load collections in separate queries.
200 would be the count with only items joined. Adding payments multiplies each row by another 3.

questions.q: Each order has 5 items. What will this query return?
questions.hint: What does LIMIT count: orders, or rows after the JOIN?

options.text: 10 orders, 5 items each
options.why: That is what you wanted, but LIMIT returns 10 rows, and 10 orders would take 50 rows.

options.text: 2 orders
options.why: LIMIT returns 10 SQL rows, and each order takes up 5, so 10 ÷ 5 = 2 orders.

options.text: 10 orders, 1 item each
options.why: The rows are sorted by order, so the first 10 rows are all the items of the first 2 orders, not 10 different orders.

options.text: Doctrine throws an exception and stops
options.why: Doctrine raises no error. It quietly returns the wrong result, which is why this trap is dangerous.

questions.q: An admin report page shows 5,000 rows: order id, customer name and total. Nothing will be changed. Which is the best fit?
questions.hint: Do you need to build full entities for data you won't change?

options.text: Fetch a DTO of three columns using DQL `NEW`
options.why: One query, only the needed columns, no entities: it saves both memory and time over 5,000 rows.

options.text: Load all the Order entities and use `fetch: EAGER` to bring the customers along
options.why: That hydrates 5,000 full entities plus their customers when you need three columns. EAGER also affects every other place that loads them.

options.text: Keep lazy loading and put a cache over the page
options.why: On a cache miss you run 5,001 queries again. The cache hides the problem rather than fixing it.

options.text: Fetch each row's customer name with a separate API call
options.why: That moves N+1 from the database onto the network, which is even slower.

questions.q: You need a list of orders with their items (to-many), paginated 20 per page. Which approaches give exactly 20 orders per page?
questions.hint: Which approaches apply LIMIT to orders, and which to the rows after the JOIN?

options.text: Use `new Paginator($query, fetchJoinCollection: true)`
options.why: Paginator first picks the ids of 20 orders, then loads them with their items via `IN (…)`.

options.text: First fetch 20 orders (with only to-one joins), then fetch their items with `IN (…)`
options.why: In the first query one order is one row, so LIMIT gives exactly 20 orders. The second query fills the collection.

options.text: Fetch-join the items and put `setMaxResults(20)` straight on it
options.why: Then LIMIT applies to the rows after the JOIN, and you get far fewer than 20 orders.

options.text: Load all the orders and cut 20 with `array_slice()` in PHP
options.why: The count would be right, but every request would pull the whole table into memory. As data grows, the server falls over.

questions.q: The nightly report pushes database CPU to 100%, and the morning orders get stuck. What is the simplest first fix?
questions.hint: The report and the orders run on the same server. Can you separate them?

options.text: Run the report on a read replica or a separate reporting copy
options.why: When the heavy query moves to another server, the primary's resources are protected.

options.text: Double the primary server's RAM
options.why: It helps for a while, but the problem returns as reports grow, and the cost goes up.

options.text: Add `LIMIT 100` to the report query
options.why: In a query with GROUP BY, the full scan finishes before the LIMIT applies.

options.text: Shut the report down
options.why: The business needs its reports. Don't stop the work; move it elsewhere.

questions.q: Which of these are OLAP work?
questions.hint: Which ones read many rows to build a summary?

options.text: Total sales by category for the last 12 months
options.why: It reads hundreds of thousands of rows and combines them; that is analysis.

options.text: Changing one order's status to `paid`
options.why: A small write to one row: that is OLTP.

options.text: A data scientist analyzing customer retention over three years
options.why: It looks for trends across a huge amount of historical data.

options.text: Looking up a user by email at login
options.why: Finding one row through an index: that is OLTP.

questions.q: What happens when you run this refresh?
questions.hint: CONCURRENTLY has a requirement. Does this view meet it?

options.text: An error: CONCURRENTLY needs a unique index on the view, and there isn't one
options.why: PostgreSQL needs a unique index to match old rows with new; without it this refresh can't run.

options.text: It succeeds, because GROUP BY makes the rows unique
options.why: Being unique is not the same as having a unique index; you have to create the index yourself.

options.text: It deletes all the rows and leaves the view empty
options.why: It doesn't empty anything; the command stops with an error at the start.

options.text: It succeeds, but locks the orders table
options.why: Locking is not the issue; the unmet requirement means the command never starts.

questions.q: After each paid order, the app also INSERTs into the warehouse itself. Why is that risky?
questions.hint: If the server dies between the two writes, what is left?

options.text: If one write succeeds and the other fails, the two places end up with different data
options.why: There is no guarantee the two writes commit together (a dual write).

options.text: Inserting into a warehouse isn't allowed
options.why: It is allowed. The trouble is keeping the two writes consistent.

options.text: INSERT is very slow
options.why: Speed isn't the main problem here; wrong totals are.

options.text: A warehouse only accepts CSV
options.why: That is a misconception; modern warehouses accept INSERTs and streams.

questions.q: Where does a database-log approach like CDC work well?
questions.hint: Where must data from one main database be kept in step elsewhere?

options.text: Keeping a search index in sync with changes in the main database
options.why: A search index is also derived data; changes from the log keep it matching the original.

options.text: Sending data from the transactional database to a warehouse in near real time
options.why: You can send just the changes instead of a full nightly dump.

options.text: Showing a customer their exact balance right now
options.why: A balance must be read straight from the source of truth, not from a derived copy.

options.text: Repairing data when something in the database gets corrupted
options.why: CDC only sends copies of changes; it doesn't repair data.

questions.q: The manager now wants revenue by city, per day. The view groups by month and category. What is the right reading?
questions.hint: What question was the view built to answer?

options.text: The view can't answer it; running the query on orders scans the whole table on the primary again
options.why: A materialized view stores the answer to one fixed query. Another question has to go back to the raw table.

options.text: REFRESH will add city and day to the view automatically
options.why: A refresh recomputes the same query; it never changes the view's columns or grouping.

options.text: A finer summary table, or a warehouse if questions keep changing, is the way out
options.why: A daily table with city serves this question cheaply; a warehouse serves any question.

options.text: Refresh the view every minute so it is always fresh
options.why: Every refresh redoes the whole calculation on the primary, so a minute-by-minute refresh would hurt checkout more.

questions.q: A Debezium connector has been stopped for a weekend, but its replication slot still exists. What is the risk?
questions.hint: Who decides when the database may delete old log files?

options.text: PostgreSQL keeps all WAL since the slot's last position, so the primary's disk can fill up
options.why: The slot tells PostgreSQL that someone still needs that log. Until the tool reads it, the files stay.

options.text: Nothing: the log is deleted after a few minutes anyway
options.why: Normally old WAL is recycled, but a slot holds it back until its reader catches up.

options.text: The reporting copy is deleted
options.why: The reporting copy simply falls behind; nothing there is deleted.

questions.q: The app runs on 2 servers. A user uploaded a photo, but it shows up sometimes and returns 404 other times. What is the likely cause?
questions.hint: Where exactly was the photo saved?

options.text: The photo is on one server's local disk and not on the other
options.why: When the load balancer sends the request to the server without the file, you get a 404.

options.text: The photo is too large
options.why: If size were the problem it would fail every time; this one is intermittent.

options.text: The CDN cache is wrong
options.why: The problem changes with the server, which points to where the file lives.

options.text: The database is slow
options.why: Slowness would cause delays; a 404 means the file wasn't found.

questions.q: What are the risks in this code?
questions.hint: The user-supplied name is used directly.

options.text: If two people upload the same name, one overwrites the other's file
options.why: A client's file name isn't unique. The key should be a server-generated UUID.

options.text: The file lives on only one server's disk
options.why: Another server, or a new deploy, won't find it.

options.text: `move()` is an old PHP method and won't work
options.why: `move()` works fine; the problem is where the file goes and what it is called.

options.text: A name containing ../ could write outside the folder
options.why: Trusting a name sent by the client is dangerous; a key the server builds itself is safe.

questions.q: What is the benefit of uploading with a presigned URL?
questions.hint: Which route does the file take?

options.text: The file goes straight to storage, saving your server's CPU, memory and network
options.why: The server only grants permission and does none of the heavy carrying.

options.text: The upload needs no verification
options.why: Verification is still needed; in the confirm step the server checks size and type.

options.text: The URL works forever
options.why: The URL has an expiry, and that is part of its security.

options.text: You can leave the bucket public to everyone
options.why: A public bucket is dangerous; presigned URLs exist precisely to avoid that.

questions.q: After the upload, the client calls `/uploads/confirm`. What is the right server behavior?
questions.hint: The client may lie.

options.text: Go to storage, check with `headObject` that the file exists and its size and type are right, then save the key
options.why: A client can be wrong by accident or on purpose, so checking for yourself is the safe route.

options.text: Save whatever the client said in the database
options.why: If the file isn't there, you collect broken references in the database.

options.text: Download every file and scan it on the server each time
options.why: That throws away the point of presigned URLs; `headObject` is enough for checking size and type.

options.text: Do nothing, because there is a URL
options.why: A URL existing is not proof that a file was uploaded.

questions.q: A 500 MB video is going up in 50 parts, and part 23 fails when the connection drops. What is the right move?
questions.hint: What happened to the other parts?

options.text: Resend only part 23 (and any that never went), then complete
options.why: The other parts are stored under the uploadId; they needn't be sent again.

options.text: Start the whole file over
options.why: That is exactly the problem multipart upload is meant to avoid.

options.text: Treat whatever arrived as the file
options.why: Without calling complete the file is never created, and with missing parts it would be corrupt.

options.text: Call complete without the ETags
options.why: Complete needs every part's number and ETag.

questions.q: A user's upload to a presigned PUT URL is 2 GB, but your limit is 5 MB. What is wrong?
questions.hint: What does a presigned PUT actually sign?

options.text: A presigned PUT can't enforce a maximum size; storage accepts the big file
options.why: The content length isn't part of the signature. Use a presigned POST with a content-length-range condition.

options.text: Nothing: the URL is time-limited, so it can't be abused
options.why: The expiry limits when, not how much. A big file within 10 minutes is still accepted.

options.text: The server should stream the file and count the bytes itself
options.why: That puts the file back through your server, which is exactly what direct upload avoids.

options.text: The client must be trusted to check the size before it uploads
options.why: A client can send anything; the limit must be enforced by storage or the server.

questions.q: Which leftovers does an unconfirmed upload create, and what cleans them?
questions.hint: The user got a URL and never called confirm.

options.text: An orphan object and a pending row, removed by a scheduled job that deletes what is still pending
options.why: The pending row is how you find the orphan object; deleting both keeps the bucket and the table clean.

options.text: Nothing is left, because storage deletes unconfirmed files by itself
options.why: Storage keeps every object it receives until something deletes it.

options.text: A broken page, fixed by the user retrying
options.why: The user never sees it, and the object keeps costing money.

questions.q: The browser refreshed at part 251 of 400 of a multipart upload. What should the page and server do?
questions.hint: Storage still holds the earlier parts under the uploadId.

options.text: Ask storage which parts it holds (ListParts), send only the missing ones, then complete from that list
options.why: Parts already stored are never sent again, and completing from storage's own list means a client can't slip in a bad part.

options.text: Start a new upload from part 1
options.why: That throws away 250 stored parts and wastes the user's time.

options.text: Complete the upload now with whatever parts the browser remembers
options.why: The file would miss parts 251 to 400, and the browser's list may be wrong.

questions.q: Thousands of `OrderPlaced` messages are sitting in the queue. A new deploy adds a required `string $currency` (no default) to the constructor. What happens?
questions.hint: The old messages have no `currency` field.

options.text: Deserializing the old messages fails, because `currency` can't be found
options.why: Without a default the object can't be built. Adding it as optional, with a default, is the right way.

options.text: Everything works; PHP fills in an empty string itself
options.why: PHP fills in nothing; a typed property with no value is an error.

options.text: Only new messages are affected
options.why: The old messages are the ones that break: the new code needs the field and they don't have it.

options.text: The queue deletes the old messages itself
options.why: A queue knows nothing about schemas; the messages will be retried and eventually land in failed.

questions.q: Which of these are usually safe changes (old readers don't break)?
questions.hint: Adding differs from changing; what could a reader fail on if it doesn't know about it?

options.text: Adding a new optional field with a default to a JSON response
options.why: A tolerant reader ignores fields it doesn't recognize.

options.text: Adding a new field in Protobuf under a new number
options.why: Old readers don't recognize the new number, so they ignore it.

options.text: Changing the type of `total_amount` from `int` to `string`
options.why: Every reader parses by type, so changing it breaks them. Add a new field instead.

options.text: Reusing the number of a removed field for a new field
options.why: Old data would be read as the value of the new field, which is wrong.

questions.q: Someone changes a field's number in the `.proto` from 2 to 7 "to keep the order tidy". What's the problem?
questions.hint: Only the number goes over the wire.

options.text: Old data is no longer recognized (the amount reads as missing) or lands in a different field, silently wrong
options.why: The number is the field's identity. Changing the number means changing the field.

options.text: Nothing; the number only affects ordering
options.why: It isn't ordering, it's identity.

options.text: It won't compile
options.why: It compiles fine, and that is the problem: the mistake is silent.

options.text: The data gets bigger
options.why: The size may shift slightly, but the real damage is the change of meaning.

questions.q: The mobile app and the server deploy at different times. The server is adding a new `mobile` field. What is the best sequence?
questions.hint: The old app still reads `phone`.

options.text: Send both `phone` and `mobile` for a while, then remove `phone`
options.why: Both app versions keep working.

options.text: Send only `mobile` and ask users to update
options.why: The app breaks for anyone who doesn't update.

options.text: Deploy the app and the API at exactly the same moment
options.why: That is impossible for an app already in the store.

options.text: Shut down the old app
options.why: That means losing customers; a safe change avoids the whole problem.

questions.q: What problem does a schema registry solve?
questions.hint: Many teams use the same topic.

options.text: Someone releasing a breaking schema without telling anyone
options.why: The registry checks compatibility before accepting a schema.

options.text: Having to send the full schema with every message
options.why: A message carries only a small schema id; the schema lives in the registry.

options.text: Slow indexes in the database
options.why: A registry has nothing to do with indexes.

options.text: Adding rate limits to an API
options.why: That is the job of an API gateway, not a registry.

questions.q: Field 4 was `string phone`, now removed. A teammate adds `string coupon_code = 4`. What happens with old messages?
questions.hint: Same number, same wire type.

options.text: Old phone numbers are read as coupon codes, with no error
options.why: The number is the identity and both are strings, so the data parses cleanly with the wrong meaning.

options.text: The compiler rejects the new field
options.why: Only a `reserved 4;` line makes it do that. Without it, this compiles.

options.text: Old messages are deleted from the queue
options.why: Messages stay as they are; only their interpretation changes.

options.text: The coupon_code is simply empty for old messages
options.why: That would be the safe outcome, but the stored value sits under number 4 and gets read.

questions.q: A team wants to rename the `orders.status` column to `state`, and deploys are rolling. What is the safest path?
questions.hint: In a rolling deploy, old and new code run side by side for a while.

options.text: Add a new `state` column, write to both, backfill, read from the new one, then drop `status`
options.why: At every step, both old and new code work.

options.text: `RENAME COLUMN` and the new code in the same release
options.why: During the deploy, old servers will look for `status`, which is gone.

options.text: Take the site down at night and rename it
options.why: That means downtime, which is unacceptable for a 24/7 service.

options.text: Just put an alias in the code and leave the column alone
options.why: That doesn't rename anything; the goal is to rename the column itself, and an alias isn't a lasting fix.

questions.q: Why will this migration cause a problem?
questions.hint: How does a Doctrine Migration run by default?

options.text: By default the migration runs in a transaction, and PostgreSQL won't allow `CONCURRENTLY` there: error
options.why: You need `isTransactional(): bool { return false; }`.

options.text: CONCURRENTLY will lock the whole table
options.why: Quite the opposite, `CONCURRENTLY` doesn't lock; the trouble is that it can't run inside a transaction.

options.text: The index will be built but nobody will use it
options.why: The command fails right away.

options.text: There is no problem
options.why: Running `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` inside a transaction makes PostgreSQL raise an error.

questions.q: Which are the safe and correct ways to fill a new column on a table with 20 million rows?
questions.hint: All at once, or in small pieces?

options.text: In batches of 1,000 rows, advancing by `id`, with pauses between them
options.why: Each lock stays short and the site keeps running.

options.text: Write the job so it can be rerun safely (an `IS NULL` condition)
options.why: If it stops halfway, you can pick up from where it left off.

options.text: Run one `UPDATE users SET mobile_number = phone`
options.why: It creates a long lock, a huge log and replica lag.

options.text: Load every row into PHP memory and save them one by one
options.why: It runs out of RAM, and every row costs a separate round trip.

questions.q: The `reference` column on a 50-million-row `payments` table is now fully populated. What is the safest way to add `NOT NULL`?
questions.hint: Keep the lock short, and do the verification separately.

options.text: Add CHECK (reference IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID, then VALIDATE, then SET NOT NULL
options.why: The heavy check runs without blocking, and the last step needs no scan (PG 12+).

options.text: Run `ALTER COLUMN reference SET NOT NULL` directly
options.why: The lock is held for the whole table scan.

options.text: Drop the table and recreate it
options.why: You would lose all the data.

options.text: Be content with adding validation in the app
options.why: Something can bypass the app and insert blanks; a database constraint is the last line of defense.

questions.q: Which statement will block writes to a 30-million-row `orders` table for as long as it takes to run?
questions.hint: Which of these does a full scan or a full build while holding a lock?

options.text: `CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user ON orders (user_id)` (plain)
options.why: A plain index build blocks every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE until it finishes. `CONCURRENTLY` avoids that.

options.text: `ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT fk_orders_user`
options.why: VALIDATE takes a weaker lock, so reads and writes carry on while it checks the old rows.

options.text: `ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT fk_orders_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users (id)` (no NOT VALID)
options.why: It checks every existing row while holding its lock. Adding it `NOT VALID` first keeps that lock short.

options.text: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_user ON orders (user_id)`
options.why: CONCURRENTLY builds the index without blocking writes. It only takes longer.

questions.q: You ran an `ALTER TABLE` at midday. Database CPU is low, yet the site is stuck. What is the most likely cause?
questions.hint: Low CPU means waiting, not working.

options.text: The ALTER holds a lock, or is waiting for one, and every query behind it is stuck
options.why: When the lock queue builds up the connection pool fills, while CPU stays low.

options.text: The database disk is full
options.why: A full disk produces write errors, and you would see other symptoms.

options.text: A bug in the new code
options.why: The timing matches the ALTER; check the database's lock list first.

options.text: A DNS problem
options.why: With DNS trouble there would be no connections at all; here connections exist but queries are stuck.

questions.q: After a sale, a product's price changes. What is the simplest way to keep old invoices correct?
questions.hint: What does an invoice rest on?

options.text: Copy the unit price into `order_items` at the time of sale
options.why: The invoice no longer depends on the product's current price.

options.text: Read `products.price` when showing the invoice
options.why: When the price changes, old invoices change too.

options.text: Forbid price changes
options.why: The business couldn't operate.

options.text: Email the customer each time
options.why: An email isn't a record, and the database holds no proof.

questions.q: Which of these rules are right for an audit_log?
questions.hint: You can't scratch things out in a ledger.

options.text: The app's database user gets INSERT permission only
options.why: Nobody can alter or delete the history.

options.text: Store the actor's id instead of the name
options.why: Names change or repeat; an id is stable.

options.text: Fix old rows with an UPDATE to keep them tidy
options.why: A correction should arrive as a new row; changing old rows destroys the value of the history.

options.text: Also keep the password hash in old_values when a password changes
options.why: Putting secrets into a log is another risk; record only the fact that "the password was changed".

questions.q: What does this query return if product 7's price went from 80 to 90 on 15 February?
questions.code:
SELECT amount FROM product_prices
WHERE product_id = 7
  AND valid_from <= '2026-02-20 10:00-05'
  AND (valid_to IS NULL OR valid_to > '2026-02-20 10:00-05');
questions.hint: Which row's period contains the date being asked about?

options.text: 90, because 20 February is after 15 February and the second row's `valid_to` is empty
options.why: The first row's `valid_to` is 15 February, which is before the 20th, so it is out. The second one matches.
The first row's period ended on 15 February; the 20th falls outside it.

options.text: Both rows
options.why: With the exclusion constraint, only one row can match at any moment.

options.text: Nothing
options.why: The second row matches.

questions.q: A users table with soft delete has a plain UNIQUE on email. Ryan deleted his account and can't register again with the same email. Why, and what is the fix?
questions.hint: The deleted row isn't really gone.

options.text: The deleted row still holds the email; build a partial unique index with `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`
options.why: Uniqueness will apply only among live rows, so deleted rows no longer get in the way.

options.text: Always hard delete; give up on soft delete
options.why: Many cases need the history; once you know the traps, soft delete is manageable.

options.text: Append a random number to the end of the email
options.why: It makes the data messy and destroys the identity of the real email.

options.text: Remove the unique constraint
options.why: Then two live users could end up with the same email.

questions.q: The admin report page shows deleted users, even though the rest of the app doesn't. What is the likely cause?
questions.hint: How is the report query written?

options.text: The report is written in native SQL or DBAL, so the Doctrine soft-delete filter didn't apply
options.why: The filter only applies to ORM/DQL queries; in native SQL you must add `deleted_at IS NULL` by hand.

options.text: Doctrine wrongly returns deleted data
options.why: The filter works fine, just not for every kind of query.

options.text: The data was never actually deleted in the database
options.why: The rest of the app doesn't show them, so `deleted_at` was set correctly.

options.text: The report is cached
options.why: Caching could be a cause, but check the native query's filter first.

questions.q: A user asks you to delete their account. By law, their orders must be kept for 7 years. What is the best action?
questions.hint: The accounts and the person are two separate things.

options.text: Keep the order rows and anonymize the personal data
options.why: The legal record survives, but the person can no longer be identified.

options.text: Delete both users and orders completely
options.why: Deleting data the law requires you to keep would break the law.

options.text: Ignore the request
options.why: You must honor a request to delete personal data; only what the law requires you to keep is excluded.

options.text: Just set `deleted_at`
options.why: With soft delete, the personal data stays; nothing is removed.

questions.q: Which of these are likely places holding copies of a user's data that `DELETE FROM users` doesn't touch?
questions.hint: Which systems take copies of data?

options.text: Elasticsearch or another search index
options.why: It is a separate copy and doesn't sync deletions by itself.

options.text: Nightly backups
options.why: They are old snapshots; the data stays until they expire.

options.text: App logs, if emails were written to them
options.why: Logs are separate files; deleting from the database doesn't change them.

options.text: The `id` column of the deleted `users` row
options.why: That row is gone.

questions.q: Look at the code: what is the biggest risk in this purge job?
questions.hint: What if the table has 50 million rows?

options.text: One huge DELETE: a long lock, a huge transaction log and replica lag
options.why: Deleting in small batches keeps each lock brief.

options.text: Nothing will be deleted, because there is no `LIMIT`
options.why: DELETE works fine without LIMIT; the problem is its size.

options.text: It is against the law
options.why: Deleting logs past their retention period is part of the policy; the question is only about the method.

options.text: The `:c` parameter won't work
options.why: The parameter binding is fine.

questions.q: Which of these follow data minimization?
questions.hint: Take less, risk less.

options.text: Checking that the user is 18+ without storing the full date of birth
options.why: Keep only what the check needs.

options.text: Asking only for an email for a newsletter, not a phone number
options.why: You don't need the phone number, so it is better not to take it.

options.text: Asking for a Social Security number on every form "in case it's useful later"
options.why: Collecting data on a guess about the future is the opposite of minimization.

options.text: Keeping all data forever so it can be analyzed later
options.why: Unlimited retention raises both risk and cost.

questions.q: Ryan's team deleted a user this morning. In the afternoon the database crashed and was restored from last night's backup. What can happen, and what should have been kept to prevent it?
questions.hint: A backup is a snapshot from before the deletion.

options.text: The deleted user comes back; with an `erasure_log` kept outside that database, you can anonymize them again
options.why: A backup is an old snapshot, and a list kept inside the same database would be rolled back with it. Keep the list of deletions elsewhere.

options.text: Nothing; a backup automatically leaves out deleted data
options.why: A backup doesn't remember events; whatever was there comes back.

options.text: Only the search index comes back
options.why: The database rows are what come back.

options.text: The restore fails automatically
options.why: The restore succeeds, which is why the risk is silent.

questions.q: Finance said $420,000 and Marketing said 4,500,000; each counted from their own copy. What fixes the root problem?
questions.hint: Before reconciling numbers, look at the definition and the source.

options.text: One `mart` table in one warehouse with a single definition, which everyone reads from
options.why: With one source and one definition, everyone gets the same number.

options.text: Ask each department to refresh its own copy more often
options.why: If the definitions differ, refreshing won't make the numbers match.

options.text: Buy a more powerful database server
options.why: The problem is the definition, not the speed.

options.text: Stop Marketing from giving out numbers
options.why: That hides the problem; it doesn't solve it.

questions.q: Which of these are characteristics of a data lake?
questions.hint: How is grain kept in a silo?

options.text: Raw data can be stored exactly as it is
options.why: Images, logs, JSON and CSV can all be kept.

options.text: It usually uses cheap object storage
options.why: So the cost is low.

options.text: Every piece of data must have a schema before it is written
options.why: That is a warehouse trait; in a lake the schema is applied at read time.

options.text: It doesn't matter if it gets messy
options.why: Without organization it becomes a "data swamp" where nobody can find anything.

questions.q: Why does the ELT extract command use `WHERE updated_at >= :s` (greater than or equal), not `>`?
questions.hint: What happens if two rows change at the same instant?

options.text: So that rows with the same timestamp aren't lost if they arrive after the previous run; duplicates are removed in staging
options.why: At-least-once: some rows may arrive twice, but none are lost.

options.text: To fetch more rows and speed things up
options.why: It is for correctness, not speed.

options.text: Writing `>` causes a SQL syntax error
options.why: `>` is valid; the problem is losing rows on the boundary.

options.text: To catch DELETEd rows
options.why: DELETEd rows can't be caught using `updated_at`.

questions.q: For fraud detection, a purchase must be blocked within a few seconds. Which kind fits?
questions.hint: How fast must the reaction be?

options.text: Streaming
options.why: You must act the moment each event happens.

options.text: A nightly batch
options.why: If it is caught the next morning, the money is already gone.

options.text: A monthly report
options.why: That isn't meant for instant reaction.

options.text: No pipeline is needed
options.why: The decision depends on analyzing events, so there is a pipeline regardless.

questions.q: Which are good governance practices?
questions.hint: When data causes trouble, who do you call, and how do you catch it early?

options.text: A team owner and a written definition for each dataset
options.why: Responsibility and meaning are clear.

options.text: Automatic checks for freshness and negative values
options.why: Bad data is caught before it reaches a dashboard.

options.text: Write permission on every dataset for everyone
options.why: If anyone can change data without an owner, trust in it disappears.

options.text: Passing metric definitions around by word of mouth
options.why: If it isn't written down and in the catalog, everyone assumes their own version.

questions.q: The extract loads the file into the warehouse first and moves the watermark afterwards. Why that order?
questions.hint: What should happen if the load fails?

options.text: If the load fails, the watermark hasn't moved, so the rerun covers the same rows
options.why: The worst case after a crash is duplicates, which staging removes. No row is skipped.

options.text: Moving the watermark first is faster, and the order makes no difference
options.why: If the load then fails, the watermark has already passed those rows and they are never extracted again.

options.text: Staging can restore rows that were never loaded
options.why: Staging only removes duplicates. A row that never reached raw can't be recovered from it.

options.text: The warehouse refuses a file until the watermark has moved
options.why: The warehouse knows nothing about the watermark; it just loads the file it is given.

questions.q: The mart sums revenue per day using updated_at. An order placed on 1 March ships on 3 March. What goes wrong?
questions.hint: Which date says when the sale happened?

options.text: Its revenue lands on 3 March, so the daily numbers are wrong; group by created_at
options.why: updated_at changes whenever the order changes. The sale belongs to the day it was created.

options.text: Nothing: the newest date is always the right one
options.why: The newest date picks the latest version of a row, not the day of the sale.

options.text: The order is counted twice
options.why: Staging keeps one row per order, so it is counted once, just on the wrong day.
